sections.title_en: The Prohibitions of Nevela and Tereifa
sections.body_en:
The Torah permitted eating the meat of kosher domestic animals, wild animals and birds, on condition that they were slaughtered according to halakha; but if the animal died of disease or in an accident, or was slaughtered not according to halakha, it becomes a nevela and it is forbidden to eat it. And even one that was slaughtered according to halakha, if a defect or wound is found in one of its organs that causes the animal's death, the sheḥita does not have the power to permit its meat for eating, for since death is already gnawing at its body, it is a tereifa. This is what is stated (Shemot 22:30): "And you shall be holy men to Me, and you shall not eat flesh torn (tereifa) in the field; you shall cast it to the dogs."1

The Sages said (Ḥullin 43a): "Eight kinds of tereifot were told to Moshe at Sinai," and they are: 1) Derusa (clawed) — the animal was clawed by the claws of a predator. 2) Nekuva (perforated) — a hole developed in one of its vital organs, such as the lung, brain, esophagus or heart. 3) Ḥasera (lacking) — from birth it lacks one of its vital organs, such as one of the lobes of the lung. 4) Netula (removed) — as a result of disease or an accident it has lost one of its vital organs, such as the liver. 5) Keru'a (torn) — a tear occurred in vital parts of its body, such as the flesh covering the rumen. 6) Nefula (fallen) — it fell and its organs were crushed.

7) Pesuka (severed) — vital organs in it were cut across their width, such as the spinal cord or the windpipe. 8) Shevura (broken) — for example, most of the animal's ribs were broken, or the thigh was dislocated from its place. In greater detail, the Sages said that there are eighteen kinds of tereifot (Ḥullin 42a), and in still greater detail the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Sheḥita 10:9-11) that there are seventy tereifot in domestic and wild animals, and seventy-two in birds (the laws of tereifot are explained in SA YD, chapters 29-60).

A domestic animal or bird that is inclined to die because of old age or because its strength has weakened, without there being a particular defect in one of its organs, is not considered a tereifa, since it is about to die in the manner of other animals, and after sheḥita it is permitted to eat its meat. Not only that, but even an animal that became ill and is in a dangerous condition, so that they hasten to slaughter it lest it die before they manage to slaughter it and become forbidden as a nevela, is permitted to eat, since it is not certain that it will die. However, it is a pious practice not to eat of its meat (Ḥullin 44b; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 4:11-12).

It is possible to explain the prohibition of tereifa in that the meat of animals contains animal forces that may draw the person who eats it downward, toward physicality, and distance him from spirituality and holiness. When the animal is whole in its body, the mitzva of sheḥita has the power to elevate its meat from animality, so that it can help Israel live a life of holiness within this world. But when it is not whole, and because of a defect in its body death has already begun to gnaw at it, the sheḥita does not have the power to elevate its meat, and if Israel eat it their souls will be damaged and they will not be able to be holy men.

notes_en.en: The verse is not speaking of an animal that was killed by a predator, for an animal that died without sheḥita is forbidden because of the prohibition of nevela, as it is stated (Devarim 14:21): "You shall not eat anything that dies of itself (nevela)." Rather, it is speaking of an animal that a predator clawed with its claws and that managed to escape. Although the animal remained alive, if it is about to die because of the clawing, it becomes a tereifa. But it is permitted to derive benefit from it, and therefore it is permitted to cast it to the dog. Clawing by a predator is only an example of a wound or defect that causes death, for every domestic animal, wild animal and bird whose flesh has a wound that is about to kill it becomes a tereifa and is forbidden to eat (see Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 4:6-8; Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 29:8-10).

sections.body_en:
Although the eight types of defects that render an animal tereifa were transmitted to Moshe at Sinai, the Tanna'im disagreed about how long a tereifa animal can continue to live. Some say only thirty days. On the other hand, some hold that it can live even two or three years. And the opinion of most of the Sages is that an animal that has become tereifa can live up to twelve months and no more. The Sages further disagreed: some hold that a female tereifa can conceive and give birth, and if it is a bird, produce eggs and lay them, and some hold that it cannot (Ḥullin 57b).

The halakhic ruling is that whenever we are in doubt whether a particular animal has become tereifa, then if it lives more than twelve months, or in the case of a female — conceives and gives birth, or in the case of a female bird — produces eggs and lays them, this is a sign that they are not tereifa, for the overwhelming majority of tereifot cannot live more than twelve months or bear young. But when it is clear that a defect that renders tereifa occurred in the animal or bird, they have the status of tereifa even if they continue to live more than twelve months and give birth or lay eggs. This is because the principles of tereifot transmitted to Moshe at Sinai, and the details of the laws that the Sages learned from them, are the essence of the halakha, whereas the rule that a tereifa does not live more than twelve months and does not give birth is intended to help only in cases of doubt (SA YD 57:18).

Similarly, if veterinarians claim that one of the types of tereifa established by the Sages does not cause the animal's death within twelve months, its law still remains that of a tereifa. And likewise, conversely, if they claim that a certain defect which according to the Sages does not render tereifa in fact causes death within a year, according to halakha this defect does not render tereifa. This is because the Torah gave the Sages the authority to decide the laws of the Torah, as it is stated (Devarim 17:11): "According to the Torah which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, you shall do; you shall not turn aside from the word which they shall declare to you, to the right or to the left" (Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 10:12-13). Therefore, what the Sages established to be tereifa is tereifa, and what they established not to be tereifa is not tereifa.2

notes_en.en:
In Ḥullin 42a, in the Mishna: "This is the rule: any [animal] with a defect such that one like it cannot live is a tereifa." And in the Gemara: "Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: … Where is there an allusion in the Torah that a tereifa does not live? … For it is written (Vayikra 11:2): 'This is the living creature (ha-ḥaya) which you may eat' — eat one that lives, but do not eat one that does not live; from this we infer that a tereifa does not live." In Ḥullin 57b it is explained that according to Rabbi, a tereifa cannot live more than thirty days, and according to the Sages a tereifa can live even two and three years and more, and this is also the opinion of Rabbi Yannai (Nidda 24a) and Rava (Temura 11b). And according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar a tereifa lives up to twelve months, and Rav Huna said that this is the halakha.
From the fact that the Tanna'im disagreed about how long a tereifa can live, it is implied that the rule ruled in halakha, that a tereifa does not live twelve months and does not bear young, is not absolute and does not define the essence of tereifa. And so wrote the Me'iri (Ḥullin 42a) and the Maharshal (Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin ch. 3, §80), that the overwhelming majority of tereifot do not manage to live twelve months or to conceive and give birth, but there are exceptions that do manage; therefore, any animal known to be a tereifa remains forbidden even if it lives twelve months. Only in a case of possible tereifa, if they lived twelve months or conceived and gave birth, are they kosher. And so explained Rabbeinu Gershom, Rashi, Rivevan, Nimukei Yosef on Ḥullin 57b, Ramban, Rashba and Ran on Ḥullin 42a; Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 11:1; and others. Thus, the words of Rav Huna, who said: "The sign of a tereifa is twelve months" (Ḥullin 57b), apply to a situation of possible tereifa, but a certain tereifa remains forbidden even if it lives for years. And the Dagul Me-revava (29:1) explained that this is the meaning of the words of Ulla (Ḥullin 43a): "Eight tereifot were told to Moshe at Sinai" — that these tereifot are forbidden in any case.
The Rashba (Responsa 1:98) holds that regarding all the laws transmitted to Moshe at Sinai, it is an absolute rule that they are tereifa and cannot live more than twelve months, and anyone who disputes this is slandering the Sages, and one should not rely on the words of physicians if they contradict the Sages. However, regarding situations of possible tereifa, or tereifot that the Sages added, if the animal lives more than twelve months, it can be permitted. And so wrote the Rivash §447. Their view is difficult, for in practice we know that there are tereifot that live more than twelve months. The Ḥazon Ish (YD 5:3) and Igrot Moshe (ḤM 2:73:4) explained that indeed all the words of the Sages are correct, and there was no tereifa that lived more than twelve months or gave birth, but today natures have changed, and there are some that live longer, as the physicians say. However, the practical halakha was established according to the condition of animals from the time of the giving of the Torah until the end of the Talmudic period, for until then natures had not changed. End of quote. However, it appears from the Rambam (Hilkhot Sheḥita 10:12-13) that the foundation of the laws of tereifa was transmitted to Moshe at Sinai, and the Sages established their details according to their understanding, based on what was known in their time; and even if it should become clear that they assessed a certain defect as more or less severe than it is assessed today, the halakha does not change, because the authority to establish halakha was given to the Great Beit Din in Jerusalem. The law of tereifa does not depend on the exact length of time the animal can continue to live, for there are Tanna'im who hold that a tereifa lives more than a year or less than thirty days; rather, the main point is that what the Sages regarded as a severe wound or defect is what renders tereifa.
Nevertheless, we find in the poskim that when it is patently clear that a certain defect is fatal and has no cure, even though it is not mentioned in the Talmud, it renders tereifa (see Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 8:23, regarding a removed upper jaw; Kesef Mishneh there; and see SA YD 33:2). The reason it was not mentioned in the Talmud is that the Sages listed tereifot that involve a novelty, but defects that clearly kill the animal they did not list (Tevu'ot Shor, Kreti, Pri Megadim, Gra YD 33:2, based on Responsa of the Rambam, Pe'er Ha-dor 29). And some say that anything not mentioned in the words of the Sages is not tereifa (Tur YD 33).

sections.body_en:
When a veterinarian performed an operation during which he cut in a place that renders tereifa, and afterwards sutured it in a way that causes the animal no harm whatsoever — some say that the animal is tereifa, since it was tereifa for a moment, and suturing performed by a person does not restore it to its kosher status. And some say that since the doctor sutured the cut in a way that will cause it no harm, it is not tereifa.3

When the surgical cut was in a place about which the poskim disagree whether it renders tereifa — for example, an animal that had difficulty giving birth was operated on by Caesarean section, or the rumen of an animal was punctured in order to release gases that had accumulated in its belly and endangered its life (as explained below, section 10) — if in practice the operated animal continued to live twelve months or gave birth, even according to the stringent opinion it can be regarded as kosher. Not only that, but according to many, if we know that all animals that undergo this operation continue to live twelve months and can conceive, as has already been the case with thousands of animals, then reality decides the dispute, that the halakha follows the lenient opinion, and there is no need to wait twelve months after each such operation.

On the other hand, there are those who are stringent and hold that only those animals that in practice lived more than twelve months or conceived have left the category of tereifa and become kosher; but one should not determine on the basis of thousands of cases that the halakha follows the lenient opinion. And some are even more stringent and hold that if the law of the animal is the subject of a dispute among the poskim, then even regarding a single animal that continued to live twelve months and conceived one should not be lenient, but rather rule according to the rules of halakhic decision alone. For according to those who forbid, these animals are certainly tereifa, and when the tereifa status is certain, even if it lives twelve months and conceives, it remains tereifa. This question is fundamental to the dispute about adhesions of the lung and the law of 'kosher' and 'ḥalak' (below, section 8).4

notes_en.en:
In Ḥullin 48a it is explained that a lung that was perforated and afterwards the hole was sealed is kosher. According to the Ramban (ibid. 76a) the reason for the permission is that a tereifa that recovered returns to its kosher status, and therefore in his opinion human action can also render a tereifa kosher; for example, an animal that became tereifa because its leg was cut at the place of the tzomet ha-gidim (the juncture of the sinews) — if before the sheḥita they cut its leg in the shank above the tzomet ha-gidim, it will become kosher again. However, the halakha was ruled not in accordance with the Ramban (SA YD 55:1; Gra there 3). For only when the healing was done by Heaven, such as a lung that was perforated and sealed, is it healed of its tereifa status, but through human action it cannot be rendered kosher (Rosh, Ḥullin 4:7); or because from the beginning of that hole in the lung its cure was beside it, and consequently it is proven that it did not render the animal tereifa (Rashi and Ran).
Following from this, the Aḥaronim disagreed about the law of an operation in the course of which a cut that renders tereifa was made, but it was sutured in a way that the animal returned to its health as before. Some say that it is kosher because it returns to health, and the repair was already planned at the time the operation was performed; and all that the Rishonim disagreed about is a situation where it did not fully return to health, for example, where its leg was cut above the tzomet ha-gidim (Si'aḥ Naḥum YD 44; Shulḥan Ha-levi 15-16). And some say that it is tereifa, for according to the Rosh it is kosher only if it heals by itself, and so too they understood the words of Rashi and Ran (Mishneh Halakhot 13:113; Rav Weitman, Teḥumin 22, p. 462; Tzitz Eliezer 1:24).

Some say that the twelve-month determination helps only regarding a doubt in the facts, but not regarding a dispute among the poskim, for according to the stringent opinion it is a certain tereifa, and twelve months do not help (Da'at Kedoshim YD 35:29; Emek Halakha YD 8; Mishpetei Uziel 2:3). However, according to the overwhelming majority of poskim, just as when there is a doubt whether a particular animal became tereifa, if it lives twelve months or gives birth it is kosher, so too when there is a dispute among the poskim regarding a particular kind of tereifa, if it lives twelve months or gives birth it is kosher (Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo Ḥullin 3:80; Shakh there 48; Pri Ḥadash YD 57:50; Torat Zevaḥ; Kreti U-pleti there 10; Ḥikrei Lev; Pri Megadim; Ḥatam Sofer; Maharam Schick; Pri Tevu'a; Ḥokhmat Adam, Sha'ar Issur Ve-heter 14:29; Zivḥei Tzedek; Beit Yitzḥak; Melamed Le-ho'il; and many others).
Not only that, but many hold that if we are certain that this defect about which the poskim disagreed does not in practice cause death, since thousands upon thousands of animals with this defect live more than twelve months and conceive and give birth, it can be decided that the halakha follows the lenient opinion (Ḥatam Sofer 5:35; Sho'el U-meshiv 1:3:81; Ateret Shlomo 16:7). This also emerges from those who permit, initially, rubbing adhesions on the basis of experience that the animals do not die (Beit Efrayim; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 39:110). On the other hand, some say that only regarding a particular animal can one be lenient if it lived twelve months or conceived, but one cannot decide in principle on the basis of reality that the halakha follows the lenient opinion (Ḥikrei Lev 1, YD 25; Pri Tevu'a YD 2; Beit Yitzḥak YD 1:61:12). However, it appears that they too were stringent because they were not certain that the reality had been properly examined, but had the matter been proven, they might have been lenient.

sections.title_en: Inspection for Tereifot and Inspection of the Lungs
sections.body_en:
Every animal that was slaughtered according to halakha has a presumption (ḥazaka) of permissibility, and it is permitted to eat its meat initially without checking whether it has one of the kinds of tereifot that the Sages enumerated. And although a small percentage of animals have defects that render them tereifa, as long as we do not know about them, there is no prohibition. For the rule is that we follow the majority, and since the overwhelming majority of animals do not have defects that render them tereifa, all animals that were slaughtered according to halakha have a presumption of being kosher. And although generally, when it is possible to check whether a certain thing is permitted or forbidden, the Sages instructed to be stringent and not rely on the majority — here, where the overwhelming majority of animals are kosher, and on the other hand checking all of them is an enormous burden, the Sages were not stringent to check all animals for all possible kinds of tereifot. Only if a concern arose about a particular organ must it be checked. For example, an animal that was struck by an arrow — one must check the injured area, lest a hole was created in it that renders it tereifa. Likewise, an animal that fell — one must check its organs lest they were damaged. Likewise, if by chance, in the course of cutting the meat, a defect was discovered, one must check whether it renders tereifa. But without a specific concern having arisen, there is no need to check the animals for the tereifot that the Sages enumerated. And so we learn from the source of the prohibition of tereifa in the Torah, as it is stated (Shemot 22:30): "And you shall be holy men to Me, and you shall not eat flesh torn (tereifa) in the field." That is, when a predator attacked an animal but did not manage to kill it, that animal requires inspection, lest a defect occurred in it that made it tereifa. From here we learn that whenever a concern has arisen that a defect may have occurred in the animal's body, one must check whether it became tereifa, but when no concern has arisen, there is no need to check (Ḥullin 9a).

However, regarding the lungs, the ruling is that they must be inspected, lest they have adhesions (sirkhot; benign growths) that may indicate a hole in the lung. And although the substantial majority of animals are not tereifa, and therefore cows have a presumption of being kosher for us, and therefore all Jews may drink cow's milk without being concerned that the cow's lung has an adhesion that renders it tereifa, nevertheless after sheḥita the ruling is that the lungs must be inspected. There are two main reasons for this: first, tereifot of the lungs are more common and are considered a prohibition of which there is a 'mi'ut ha-matzui' (a common minority), and according to the Sages, when it is possible, one is obligated to check it (Rashi). Second, since adhesions are noticeable and prominent, if they are not inspected, people will end up in complicated situations. For when they are discovered by the buyers, they will need to ask a sage about them, and if it turns out that they are tereifot, they will need to search for all the buyers of the meat of that animal in order to separate them from the prohibition. And one who has begun cooking the meat will need to throw out his entire dish and kasher the pot, and perhaps because of the loss and the trouble he will be negligent about it. Therefore, they ruled not to eat or sell the meat of a domestic or wild animal without first inspecting its lungs. In addition, since they are noticeable and prominent, if they do not inspect them, they will appear to be turning a blind eye to the prohibition (Rashba, Ḥullin 9a).

If before they managed to inspect the lungs they threw them away by mistake, or a dog came and ate them, it is permitted to eat the meat of the domestic or wild animal, because in such a situation one returns to the basic rule that we follow the majority, and most animals are kosher. Some are lenient about this only in a case of great loss (SA and Rema YD 39:2). And if the lungs were deliberately lost before their inspection, it is forbidden to eat the meat of that animal (Shakh 6).5

notes_en.en:
The Talmud does not state that there is an obligation to inspect the lungs, but rather that those who eat of the meat before they have seen the lungs are behaving improperly (Beitza 25b, and Rashi). According to many, inspection of the lungs is an obligation by rabbinic law, according to the rule that wherever there is a 'mi'ut ha-matzui' of a prohibition, although by Torah law we follow the majority, by rabbinic law, when it is possible to check, one is obligated to check. Only when the prohibition is a 'mi'ut she-eino matzui' (an uncommon minority) is there no obligation to check it (Ramban, Rashba, Ran, Tashbetz). And so wrote the Aḥaronim as halakha (Radbaz 4:112; Rema 39:17; Shakh 8; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 5; and others). And some say that there is no rabbinic obligation to inspect the lungs; rather, inspecting the lungs is a stringent custom that spread throughout Israel until it became a binding custom (Me'iri, Ḥullin 9a; Mordekhai, Ḥullin 619, in the name of Rabbeinu Barukh; and this is also implied by Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 11:7, 13, 14). Their view can be explained in several ways: either that in their opinion, if the percentage of tereifot were at the level of a 'mi'ut ha-matzui' there would be an obligation to inspect them, but in practice the percentage of tereifot does not reach the level of a 'mi'ut ha-matzui'. Or that the percentage of tereifot is at the level of a 'mi'ut ha-matzui', but since this inspection involves great trouble, there is no obligation to perform it (as in the view of Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 17, cited below 23:6). Or that they follow the view of some of the Rishonim who hold that even by rabbinic law there is no obligation to check a 'mi'ut ha-matzui' (Rashi, Rashbam and Tosafot, below 23:6). Or because from the time the animal was slaughtered properly, it has a presumption of being kosher.
In any case, even according to those who hold that there is a rabbinic obligation to inspect the lungs, according to most of the Rishonim, if the lungs were lost inadvertently before they were inspected, the animal is kosher. And so wrote the Rosh, Ran, Rambam, the author of the Ittur, and Rashba, and so it was ruled in SA YD 39:2. And according to the Behag, the Mordekhai in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak Ha-levi, and the Ra'avan — it is forbidden (since it has already become customary to inspect them, it has lost its presumption of being kosher, or because they feared that people might throw them away deliberately). See below, note 9, regarding the law in a situation where most animals have adhesions.

sections.title_en: What Is an Adhesion of the Lung
sections.body_en:
Adhesions (sirkhot) are growths that cling to and spread over the surface of the lung and create attachments extending from one place on the surface of the lung to another place on the surface of the lung, or create attachments between the surface of the lung and the wall of the chest or one of the organs adjacent to the lungs. The reason an adhesion renders tereifa is that it forms from a hole that was in the lung, and although the adhesion seals it, later it will detach and the hole will remain open and cause the animal's death (Rashi). And some say that the adhesion did not form from a hole, but as a result of the stretching of the adhesion it will be torn from the lung and a hole will remain beneath it that will cause the animal's death (Tosafot). However, only an adhesion that is 'she-lo ke-sidran' (not in their natural order) renders tereifa, because it adheres between two places that are not adjacent to each other, and causes the surface of the lung to stretch when the animal breathes, until in the end the adhesion will be torn away and a hole will remain beneath it that will cause the animal's death. But if the adhesion is 'ke-sidran' (in their natural order), that is, it adheres between two places that are in any case adjacent to each other, it is kosher, because when the animal breathes it does not cause unnatural stretching of the surface of the lung, and consequently there is no concern that a hole will form there (Ḥullin 46b).6

In general, there are two disputes regarding the law of adhesions. The first: where is the location of the kosher adhesions that are 'ke-sidran', and where is the location of the tereifa ones that are 'she-lo ke-sidran'. The second, which is the more important one in practice: is an adhesion that is 'she-lo ke-sidran' always tereifa, or is only an adhesion with a hole beneath it tereifa, and in order to check this one must perform a bubbling test or a test of rubbing and handling. In the first dispute, Rabbi Yosef Karo is lenient and the Rema is stringent. In the second, which determines the law of most animals, Rabbi Yosef Karo is stringent and the Rema is lenient.

The first dispute: the animal's lung is divided into lobes (unot), that is, spaces into which the air enters. Una means 'ear' in Aramaic, and because of the resemblance of the parts of the lung to drooping ears, they were called unot. On the right side there are four lobes, and on the left side three lobes, with each side having one large lobe called the 'uma', from the word for the mother (em) of the lobes. When the lung fills with air, the lobes press against one another, and only a slit is visible between them.

Some say that whenever the adhesions adhere between two parts adjacent to each other in a way that is not visible from the outside — for example, two sides of lobes that press against each other, or where in the narrow place of the chest adhesions attach the lung to the chest wall — these adhesions do not render tereifa at all, and there is no need to check them (Rashba; SA YD 39:4; 18).

On the other hand, some are stringent and hold that only if the adhesion connects two adjacent lobes in the inner half of the slit between them is it considered ke-sidran and cannot render tereifa. But if it is in the outer half, and likewise when it adheres from the lung to the chest wall, even in the narrow front part, it is already liable to create a certain stretching of the surface of the lung when the animal breathes, and therefore it is considered 'she-lo ke-sidran' and renders tereifa (Mahari Weil, and Rema 39:4; 18).7

notes_en.en: According to Rashi (Ḥullin 46b), the adhesion forms from fluids that come out of a hole in the surface of the lung, and even if the hole becomes sealed, when the adhesion is not in its natural order it will eventually come apart and the hole will open. And according to Tosafot (there, s.v. 'haynu'), there is an adhesion that forms without a hole, but since it is attached not in its natural order, there is a presumption that it will stretch the surface of the lung until a hole forms in it. Doctors today hold that adhesions are caused by pneumonia, which causes the surface of the lung to become permeable, and various substances come out of the lung and accumulate on its surface, creating growths and thick membranes ('Ma'or La-kashrut' vol. 3, p. 126). The older the animal, the higher the chance that it has adhesions.

Another, very lenient view was practiced in Morocco and in many communities in North Africa, according to which an adhesion extending from one lobe to an adjacent lobe, even from back to back, does not render tereifa and does not require inspection, and if it extended from one lobe to another, skipping over a lobe between them — it renders tereifa (as explained in detail in 'Divrei Shalom Ve-emet' vol. 4, p. 148). Today, since it is easy to obtain meat that is kosher according to most poskim, no one practices leniency in this.

sections.body_en:
The second dispute concerns adhesions that are 'she-lo ke-sidran', which are the tereifa ones, and it relates to two issues: 1) Whether it is possible to peel off the adhesion and check whether there is a hole beneath it, and on the basis of this check to declare the adhesion kosher. 2) Whether adhesions that can be removed by rubbing and handling are considered adhesions that render tereifa.

We will begin with the first issue. Some say that when the adhesion is 'she-lo ke-sidran', the animal is tereifa in any case. And even if they remove it and find that there is no hole beneath it, it is tereifa, because even if it is sealed now, it will eventually open (Rabbeinu Gershom, Rif, Rashi and Tosafot on Ḥullin 48a).

On the other hand, some say that even when the adhesion is 'she-lo ke-sidran', this does not mean that it is tereifa, but rather that it must be checked, and if a hole is found beneath it, it is tereifa. To check the adhesion, one can peel it off with a knife, or cut it into strips and gently peel them off by hand, for the adhesion resembles nylon and can be broken down into thin threads and stretched until they peel off the surface of the lung. After the surface of the lung has been left smooth, one inflates it with air and puts it into water; if air bubbles come out of it, it has a hole and the animal is tereifa. And if there is no bubbling, there is no hole in it and the animal is kosher, because only an adhesion with a hole beneath it renders tereifa (Maharitz, based on Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 11:6-9; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 110-111).8

notes_en.en:
Ḥullin 48a: "Rav Neḥemya son of Rav Yosef would check it (a lung that adhered by means of an adhesion to the chest wall) in lukewarm water" (inflating the lung and putting it into lukewarm water to check whether air bubbles come out of the lung). And according to Mar Zutra son of Rav Huna son of Rav Pappi, Rav Neḥemya would check adhesions between two lobes of the lung in this way. And Rav Ashi raised a difficulty against Mar Zutra. The overwhelming majority of the Rishonim ignored the opinion of Mar Zutra, implying that they held that the check in lukewarm water is intended only for an adhesion between the lung and the chest wall. Some of them said that this check is effective only when there is an abnormality (ri'uta) in the chest from which the adhesion presumably extended, but if there is no abnormality, the check is not effective (Rif, Rashi, Tosafot, Rabbeinu Gershom); and some say that if there is an abnormality in the chest — the animal is kosher without a check, and if there is no abnormality, it is kosher only if it is checked and does not bubble (Rabbeinu Tam, Ra'zah).
On the other hand, the custom of the sages of Yemen, from the days of the Rambam, was to remove all the adhesions that are 'she-lo ke-sidran' and check them by bubbling, as cited in the Responsa of Rabbi Avraham son of the Rambam 61, in a response to the sages of Yemen. And the Maharitz (Zevaḥ Toda YD 39:88) explained that this is the opinion of the Rambam, Hilkhot Sheḥita 11:6-7, that the halakha follows Mar Zutra, that Rav Neḥemya's check is effective for all adhesions. And so many practiced in Ashkenaz and in North Africa, as explained in the next note, according to the principle that only if it turns out that there is a hole beneath the adhesion is the animal tereifa. It is possible that Rav Ashi's objection to Mar Zutra's explanation relates only to very thick adhesions surrounded by an abnormality such as pus and disease, but with ordinary adhesions, even thick ones that extend not in their natural order, he would agree that they can be peeled off and checked for bubbling beneath them.

sections.body_en:
The second issue is whether adhesions that can be removed by rubbing and handling render tereifa. Some say that when the adhesion is 'she-lo ke-sidran', the animal is tereifa in any case, even if it is the thinnest of the thin (Rashba and Rashbatz), and so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (YD 39:10): "Wherever they forbade an adhesion of the lung, there is no difference between an adhesion as thin as a hair and one that is thick, strong and as wide as a thumb; and not like those who rub it by hand, and if it was rubbed away they lean toward leniency — and whoever practices so is as though he feeds tereifot to Israel."

On the other hand, some say that an adhesion that can be removed by handling is not considered an adhesion but mucus. For this purpose one rubs, rolls and handles the adhesion. If it peels off the lung, this is a sign that it is mucus, which does not render tereifa. For "an adhesion — if a person were to rub it between his fingers all day, it would keep getting stronger" (Rosh). And as the Mahari Weil wrote: "All the adhesions that are tereifa are those that are hard, but if they dissolve when handled by hand, they are called mucus and it is kosher." However, in practice, even those who are lenient to remove the adhesions by rubbing and handling customarily check the lung afterwards by inflating it in water to see whether it bubbles (Baḥ; Shakh 39:15).9

notes_en.en: There are three levels of actions for checking adhesions: 1) According to the Ashkenazic custom, based on the Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, one is lenient with thin adhesions that detach with gentle stretching; and the Shulḥan Arukh 39:11, 13, was lenient in this only in an animal of a Jew and in a case of great loss, when the inspector is kosher and very God-fearing. (And very thin adhesions that fall off by themselves with a slight shake are permitted according to all opinions.) 2) The Ashkenazic custom is to rub and handle the adhesions, and if they peel off by this, it implies that they are not real adhesions. In this way they removed the thin adhesions and most of the medium ones. The source of this custom is in the words of the Ge'onim, as cited in Sefer Ha-me'orot in the name of Rabbi Natan son of Rabbi Meir, and it is also cited in the Me'iri in the name of the sages of Narbonne. And so wrote the Rosh, Ḥullin 47a, and the Mahari Weil, Laws of Lung Inspection §6. However, even after they have been removed by rubbing and handling, the custom is to be stringent and check these lungs for bubbling in water (Baḥ and Shakh 39:34). On the other hand, according to Rav Yehudai Gaon, the Rashba in Torat Ha-bayit Ha-arokh, Bayit 2, Sha'ar 3, 34b [?], the Tashbetz, and SA 39:10, checking by rubbing and handling is entirely forbidden. 3) In Yemen the custom was to peel off with a knife even adhesions that do not come off through rubbing and handling, and after the surface of the lung had been left smooth, they checked the lung in water for bubbling. The root of their custom is that an adhesion forbids only if there is a hole beneath it. And so they practiced in Morocco with the vast majority of adhesions. In Ashkenaz too, in the days of the Aḥaronim, the custom was to peel off large adhesions and check them by bubbling, but they preferred to remove them carefully by breaking the adhesion down into thin threads, which are gently stretched until they peel off and the surface of the lung is left smooth. And this is the practice today in all the 'kosher' hekhsherim. In Ashkenaz they added a further reason for permitting it: an adhesion that does not bubble is an external membrane that does not originate from the lung itself. In practice, the great rabbis of Ashkenaz disagreed whether it is proper to be lenient in this. The stringent: Pri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 17; Torat Yekutiel 6; Aderet Eliyahu 44, in the name of Rav Ḥayim of Volozhin; and others. The lenient, who upheld the custom: Rosh Efrayim 153, in the name of his uncle Rav Sander; Ḥatam Sofer YD 39; Tiferet Tzvi YD 4; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 39:110; Beit David 39, part 6:3-4. (And see Mazon Kasher Min Ha-ḥai pp. 326-328.)

sections.title_en: The Customs of the Communities in Practice
sections.body_en:
In all the regions around the Land of Israel, including Syria, Iraq and Egypt, the custom was to be stringent and not to rub and peel adhesions, but rather they declared tereifa every animal that had an adhesion 'she-lo ke-sidran'. On the other hand, in Yemen, Persia, Morocco, and with them many communities of Tunisia and Libya, as well as many in all the communities of Ashkenaz, the custom was to be lenient to peel, or at least to rub and handle, adhesions.

It seems that the differences in custom between the countries stemmed largely from the degree of loss involved. For since the law of adhesions is the subject of a dispute among Amora'im and Rishonim, and the doubt concerns a Torah prohibition, the prevalent ruling was to be stringent. However, in a place where it was not possible to sell the tereifa animals to a non-Jew, declaring an animal tereifa could bring disaster and ruin upon the owner of the animal, for the loss of an animal was equivalent to the loss of a month's or several months' wages, and for the poor the question touched on life itself. Therefore, in such a time of great distress, they relied on the lenient opinion.

In places where there were Sunni Muslims, the Muslims were willing to buy the tereifot, and therefore everyone practiced according to the stringent opinion, as the Rambam testified (Hilkhot Sheḥita 11:11). However, in places ruled by Shiite Muslims, such as Yemen and Persia, they regarded food touched by a Jew as impure, and were not willing to buy the tereifot, and because of the distress they practiced according to the lenient views (Maharitz in Mekor Ḥayim 31:96).

In the Christian lands of Ashkenaz too, the situation of the Jews in the days of the Rishonim was precarious, and many times they had difficulty selling the tereifot to non-Jews; therefore they practiced leniency to check thin and medium adhesions by rubbing and handling, but they were not lenient to peel thick adhesions and check them by bubbling. In Spain, as long as the war between the Christians and the Muslims had not been decided, the Christians generally behaved with a certain tolerance toward the Jews, and they could practice according to the stringent opinion, as the Rashba ruled (he lived in Barcelona, died 5070, 1310). However, as the Christians grew stronger, hostility and hatred toward the Jews increased, until they had to rely in a time of distress on the most lenient opinion, and they would check the adhesions by bubbling (Beit Yosef YD 39:22).

In the lands of North Africa they practiced according to the stringent opinion for many generations; however, after the Christian rulers of Spain expelled the Jews (5252, 1492), and many of them emigrated to North Africa, the discussion of how one should practice was renewed. In Morocco, where the great Jewish community in the lands of Islam developed, the debate erupted in full force. The veteran residents sought to be stringent according to their custom, but the expellees held that the halakha follows the lenient opinion, and that even not in a time of distress one should check all adhesions by peeling and bubbling. The dispute continued for about fifty years, until the rabbis of the expellees prevailed and the halakha was decided leniently, that the adhesions are checked. And so the custom spread in most communities of North Africa, except Algiers and Djerba, where they practiced stringency.

Similarly in Ashkenaz, in the days of the Aḥaronim it was already possible to sell the tereifot to non-Jews, and there were rabbis who came out sharply against those who were lenient regarding rubbing and handling (Shelah, Gra). And there were those who inclined to be stringent but did not want to invalidate the custom of those who were lenient (Rema, Kreti U-pleti, Levushei Serad). On the other hand, there were those who held that the main halakha follows the lenient opinion (Yam Shel Shlomo; Shakh 39:33; Simla Ḥadasha 36). And many even went further and permitted peeling thick adhesions and checking them by bubbling, like the custom of Yemen and Morocco (Ḥatam Sofer, Beit David, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 39:110).

That is to say, in the days of the Aḥaronim, even not in a time of distress, in many countries they practiced according to the lenient opinion, because they held that this is the main halakha. For the rule is that a tereifa does not live more than twelve months, and in practice they came to know that most adhesions of the lungs do not cause the death of the animals. It is a fact that many times about 80% of older cows are found to have adhesions, and it is known that if they are not slaughtered, they will continue to live several more years until they die of old age. And even in young calves, adhesions are sometimes found in about 50%, and it is clear that if they are not slaughtered, they will continue to live many years. We have already learned (section 3, n. 4) that according to many, when there is a dispute among the poskim about a certain defect, whether it renders tereifa, and it is found in practice that the animals do not die from it, one should decide on the basis of reality that the halakha follows the poskim who permit. And the stringent respond that one should not decide halakha on the basis of reality, for what has been established with certainty as rendering tereifa renders tereifa even if it turns out that the animals do not die from it.

Thus the debate has continued to our day. However, the custom of Israel is Torah, and the custom is to call meat that is found kosher according to the lenient opinion 'kosher', for this is the main ruling according to the rules of halakha. And the custom is to call meat that is found kosher according to the stringent opinion 'ḥalak' or 'glatt' (smooth).10

notes_en.en:
In the period of the Rishonim, in most communities of Israel the custom was to be stringent and not to check adhesions by bubbling, and so testified the Rambam, Rosh, Rashba and others. On the other hand, at the end of the period of the Rishonim, in Spain (Castile) and in the community of Salonika the custom was to check adhesions that are 'she-lo ke-sidran', as cited in the Beit Yosef (YD 39:22) in the name of Rabbi David Yiḥya: "Because the non-Jews in their lands most of the time … would not eat the sheḥita of Jews, and they would lose the value of the tereifa animals. And had they practiced according to the stringent opinion, there would have been a great loss to the money of Israel. But in places where the non-Jews eat from the sheḥita of Jews, one should be stringent according to the opinion of the Ramban and the Rosh and the custom of the places of the Rambam and the Rashba." In Yemen too the custom was to be lenient and check all kinds of adhesions (according to their understanding that the Rambam ruled like Mar Zutra), and so wrote Rabbi David Mishreki (Re'shei Besamim 39:21). And so wrote the Maharitz (Mekor Ḥayim 31:96): "Know that wherever we said in the law of adhesions that it is tereifa, it is not absolutely tereifa. Rather, one breaks apart the adhesion and is careful that nothing of the adhesion remains, and afterwards one checks in lukewarm water; if it does not bubble — it is kosher. And so is the ancient custom in all the lands of Yemen from ancient times, transmitted from mouth to mouth. And our fathers saw according to the law and the truth, as the Rambam wrote, because of the loss of the money of Israel, and it is sufficient for them to conduct themselves according to the law and not to be stringent."
A central argument for the lenient view is that it is known in halakha that most animals are kosher, and an ordinary slaughtered animal has a presumption of being kosher, and therefore it was ruled in the Talmud that if the lungs were lost and cannot be checked, the animal is kosher. And if we rule according to the stringent opinion regarding adhesions, it will turn out that most animals are tereifa. And the stringent respond that indeed in the past there were fewer adhesions in the lungs, and over the generations the condition of the animals changed for the worse. Moreover, this is a doubt concerning a Torah law, and one must be stringent in it. And those who permit hold that it is not reasonable that such extreme changes occurred in the condition of the animals.
It appears that even according to the custom of those who were half-lenient, that is, only with adhesions that come off through rubbing and handling, in the period of the Aḥaronim they declared tereifa a higher percentage than was accepted in the days of Ḥazal. As the Simla Ḥadasha wrote (39:1): "Most domestic animals, wild animals and birds are healthy and kosher; although nowadays we sometimes see more tereifot than kosher ones, that is because of the doubts and stringencies, and because we are not expert in the inspection of several things, but according to the strict law the majority are kosher" — and this according to the view that rubbed and handled adhesions. All the more so, according to the stringent view, the percentage of tereifot was much higher. And the Sha'agat Aryeh (64) was asked, regarding Yom Tov, that since the percentage of tereifot is like the percentage of kosher animals because of the lung inspection, how is it permitted to slaughter an animal on Yom Tov? And he answered that the reason for the tereifot in these years is "because of the stringency of the Aḥaronim, who were stringent with many stringencies in the inspection of the lung, and many of the Aḥaronim cried out like cranes about this, that they are losing the money of Israel for nothing, but it has already become the custom…" And so wrote the Pri Ḥadash (39:3), that although more tereifot than kosher animals are found, this is not according to the strict law but because of the stringency of the Aḥaronim. And see Peninei Halakha: Mo'adim 4:7.
The percentages of 'kosher' and 'ḥalak' in our day: in the book 'Ma'or La-kashrut', the part 'Preparation of Meat', pp. 104-110, 136-137, it is summarized that in Israel: beef calves aged six months to two years: 30% ḥalak, 53% kosher according to the lenient view, 17% tereifa according to all views. In older cows slaughtered after a prolonged period of milking, there is almost no ḥalak, about 40% are kosher, and 60% tereifa. Most of the meat marketed in Israel comes from South America. In Argentina, in beef calves: 35% ḥalak, 35% kosher, about 30% tereifa. Regarding small domestic animals in Israel, fewer checks have been carried out, but one of the checks showed that about 23% are tereifa, and 77% ḥalak and kosher. Most of these tereifot are from adhesions of the lung, but there are also tereifot for other reasons, the most common of which is the presence of a nail or a piece of wire in the reticulum (beit ha-kosot). From various checks it emerged that three main factors affect the percentage of adhesions: 1) The older the animal, the more the percentage of adhesions rises. 2) The poorer its rearing conditions, the more adhesions it has; and when it is not exposed to drafts and receives treatment when it catches cold, the phenomenon of adhesions decreases. 3) There are breeds in which the frequency of adhesions is higher, such as dairy breeds.

sections.body_en:
It follows, then, that there are three levels of kashrut in the meat of domestic and wild animals. 1) 'Kosher' according to the custom of Ashkenaz, Yemen and Morocco — they are lenient to peel the adhesions, and only if it turns out that there is a hole beneath them is the animal tereifa.

2) Ḥalak 'Beit Yosef', according to the view of Rabbi Yosef Karo — they are stringent not to rub, handle or peel adhesions at all, but in certain places in the lung the adhesions do not render tereifa. 3) 'Glatt' (which means smooth in Yiddish), according to the Ashkenazic custom following the rulings of the Rema — they are stringent not to rub, handle or peel adhesions at all, and are even stringent to declare tereifa adhesions that according to the 'Beit Yosef' are kosher because they are considered 'ke-sidran' (above, section 6 [?]). However, on the other hand, if the adhesion is flimsy and detaches very easily, even if it is 'she-lo ke-sidran', they remove it, whereas according to the 'Beit Yosef' one is lenient in this only in special cases, but as a rule flimsy adhesions are not removed (above, n. 9).

In practice, today the kashrut of animal meat is customarily divided into two levels: 1) 'Kosher', according to the lenient view, as many practiced in Ashkenaz, and as they practiced in Yemen, Persia, Morocco and most communities of North Africa. 2) 'Ḥalak' (or 'glatt' in Yiddish), in which one must be careful about the stringencies of both the 'Beit Yosef' and the Rema, because if they are careful only about the stringencies of the 'Beit Yosef', it will turn out that on rare occasions there will be animals there that according to the custom of the stringent in Ashkenaz would be considered tereifa. And if they are careful only about 'ḥalak' according to the Rema, it will turn out that there will be animals there that are kosher according to the 'Beit Yosef' only in a time of distress. However, some batei din tzedek practice 'ḥalak' according to the view of the Rema alone, and some practice 'ḥalak' according to the 'Beit Yosef' alone; and in a time of need, even one who is careful to eat 'ḥalak' according to one of the views may rely on the other view, because of a sefek sefeika (double doubt).

In halakhic practice, a person may follow the lenient opinion, because their opinion rests on strong reasoning; therefore this meat is called 'kosher'. Initially it is good to be meticulous and careful to eat 'ḥalak', because this enhancement is the most important one in the laws of kashrut, and one who is accustomed to be stringent in it is generally saved from many doubts, for in all kashrut systems, care about 'ḥalak' means serious supervision in all areas. It is especially fitting that one whose community or parents were accustomed to be stringent to eat 'ḥalak' should continue their custom.11

notes_en.en:
Seemingly, according to what was practiced in most communities of Israel — that when it was possible to be stringent without great loss, they were stringent according to the stringent view — today too one should be stringent, for the difference between the price of kosher meat and the price of ḥalak-glatt meat is not so great. On the other hand, however, after many communities practiced permitting it and reinforced the permission with strong arguments, today too one who wishes to rely on them may do so. And even one who has been accustomed to be stringent may decide to follow the lenient opinion, and it is preferable that he perform hatarat nedarim (annulment of vows) for this, for initially one does not rely on the general hatarat nedarim performed before the Days of Awe. However, it is fitting that one whose family was accustomed to be stringent should continue their custom. Yeshiva students who have taken upon themselves to eat 'ḥalak', and whose parents are not careful to eat 'ḥalak', should eat 'kosher' meat when they are at their parents' home (and so ruled Rav Mordechai Eliyahu, of blessed memory). For although the care to eat 'ḥalak' is important and they took it upon themselves, since the mitzva of honoring parents is more stringent, their acceptance does not obligate them in the case of a conflict with the mitzva of honoring parents. And even after their marriage, if their care to eat 'ḥalak' would cause great distress to their parents, it is better that they eat 'kosher' at their home and not hurt them. But as a rule, one who is accustomed to be careful to eat 'ḥalak' must be careful to keep his custom everywhere. And so Rav Ḥayim David Halevi, of blessed memory, ruled for soldiers who are careful to eat 'ḥalak', that in the army too they should not be lenient to eat 'kosher' (Aseh Lekha Rav 6:56). One who wishes to be stringent to eat 'ḥalak' without having taken upon himself to always practice so may eat 'kosher' when he is a guest, even without the need of honoring parents.
The Responsa Devar Shmuel 320 wrote that one who is careful to eat 'ḥalak' and comes to eat at his friend's home, who eats kosher, may eat because of a sefek sefeika: 1) perhaps the halakha follows the entirely lenient opinion regarding adhesions of the lung; 2) even if the halakha follows the stringent opinion, perhaps the meat that was served to him was 'ḥalak'. However, today one cannot argue that perhaps meat labeled 'kosher' is 'ḥalak', since all meat is sold according to its level. But some say that one may refrain from asking because of the unpleasantness, and consequently the sefek sefeika returns (Yabi'a Omer 5, YD 3). However, when 'ḥalak Beit Yosef' meat is served, one who practices ḥalak according to the Rema may eat it because of a sefek sefeika: 1) perhaps the halakha follows the lenient opinion; 2) even if the halakha follows the stringent opinion according to the Rema, it is doubtful whether it had adhesions that according to the Rema render tereifa. Likewise, if 'ḥalak' meat according to the Rema is served to one who practices according to the 'Beit Yosef', he may eat it because of a sefek sefeika: 1) perhaps the halakha follows the lenient opinion; 2) even if the halakha follows the stringent opinion, it is doubtful whether there was a flimsy adhesion there which according to the 'Beit Yosef' may be removed only in a time of distress. (See Kaf Ha-ḥayim 39:224, regarding the source of the definition of 'kosher' and 'ḥalak'. And see Responsa Ama Davar 1, §§5-7, on the levels of hekhsherim for Sephardim and Ashkenazim, and the ruling according to our master and teacher Rav Eliyahu.)

sections.body_en:
The poskim disagreed about the law of an animal that had such difficulty giving birth that it was endangered, and in a Caesarean section its womb was opened and its offspring taken out. The halakha is that an animal whose womb was removed is kosher (SA YD 45:1). However, regarding a situation where its womb was cut and perforated, some are stringent (Baḥ); some hold that initially one should be stringent and in a time of distress one may be lenient (Rema); and some are lenient even initially (Pri Ḥadash and Gra). And some say that even those who are stringent regarding a hole in the womb would be lenient if it was made in the framework of an operation by a veterinarian (Hagahot on Issur Ve-heter He-arokh 55:7:2 [?]). In halakha, it appears that these animals are kosher even initially, because in practice they continue to live twelve months and conceive and give birth, and according to many, on this basis all animals that undergo a Caesarean section can be declared kosher. In addition, some say that any animal that was operated on by a veterinarian and will eventually recover is not forbidden, even if the cut was in a place that renders tereifa (above, section 3).

Another question arose regarding an animal that ate grasses that caused gases to accumulate in its rumen, so that if it does not manage to release them, its rumen will burst and it will die. It is accepted practice in the world to puncture its rumen in the area of the ribs in order to release the gases, and afterwards the animal continues to live, conceive and give birth. The problem is that there is a dispute whether a hole in the rumen renders tereifa, and the opinion of most poskim is to be stringent. In practice, in this question too the halakha follows the lenient opinion, for in every situation of possible tereifa, if the animal continued to live twelve months or conceived, it is not tereifa. And if it has become clear that this is the situation with all animals, the halakha should be decided according to the lenient opinion (above, section 3). However, in practice, out of concern for the stringent opinion, methods have been found for releasing the dangerous gases without perforating the rumen, by inserting a tube into the esophagus. And this is the practice today with all animals raised for Jews.12

When animals are raised near human dwellings, they swallow whatever comes to their mouths, and among other things they may swallow nails that reach the reticulum (beit ha-kosot, one of the parts of the stomach). Then, if the nail made a through-and-through hole in the wall of the reticulum, the animal is tereifa (SA YD 48:1; 6-7), and it is proper that the lung inspectors pay attention to this as well.

notes_en.en:
Mishna Ḥullin 42a: "These are tereifot in a domestic animal … the inner rumen that was perforated, or most of the outer one that was torn." And in the Gemara there, 50b, the Amora'im disagreed about what the 'inner rumen' is, whose perforation in any amount renders tereifa, and what the 'outer' one is, which becomes tereifa only if most of it was torn. According to Rabba bar Rav Huna, the 'inner rumen' is the part that is revealed when the animal's belly is opened, that is, the lower and rear side, and the 'outer' is opposite the ribs and the spine, and consequently the hole for releasing the gases does not render tereifa. And according to Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, the 'inner' means that the hole is in the rumen itself on any of its sides, and the 'outer' means that the hole is in the outer flesh and did not penetrate to the rumen itself, and consequently the hole for releasing the gases renders tereifa. The Rishonim disagreed about whom the halakha follows. According to the Ittur, the Rashba in the name of the Ramban, and others, the halakha follows the lenient one. And according to Rashi, Rivevan, Rid, Rambam (Hilkhot Sheḥita 9:5), Rosh, Mordekhai and others, the halakha follows the stringent one. And so it was ruled in SA YD 48:2. However, we learned in note 4 that according to most poskim, if it lives twelve months or gives birth, one should decide according to the lenient poskim. And according to many, if it has become clear that this is the situation in thousands of animals, one should decide according to the lenient opinion even without waiting twelve months. However, some say that only in an evenly balanced dispute can one rely on the twelve-month test, but here, where most poskim were stringent, one should not be lenient (Pri Megadim, Siftei Da'at 81:5 [?]; Yehuda Ya'aleh 60). On the other hand, some say that the stringent Rishonim were stringent because of the doubt, and consequently according to them too, if it lives twelve months it will be kosher (Pitḥei Teshuva YD 48:2; Yabi'a Omer 8, YD 2). Moreover, one could say that had they known that in practice animals continue to live with such holes for more than twelve months, they would have decided according to the lenient opinion.
There is another medical treatment: 'stomach reversal', intended for cows whose stomach has turned over to the point that they cannot continue to eat. When their stomach is turned back, it is sutured to the wall so that it will not turn over again; according to the stringent view, one must take care that the stomach is not perforated during the suturing. And according to the lenient view, even if its stomach is perforated, since this is done by a veterinarian who looks after the cow's health, there is no concern of tereifa, as shown by the fact that the cows afterwards live more than twelve months.

sections.title_en: The Kashrut of Poultry and the Question of Vaccinations
sections.body_en:
Following the need to vaccinate poultry against diseases, a concern arose that the prick of the vaccination needle in the breast might reach the cavity of the esophagus, the stomach or the lungs and render the bird tereifa (SA YD 33:3; 35:1). Indeed, there were cases in which unskilled workers administered the injections, and many chicks died because of them. However, following the mishaps that occurred at first, the poultry growers improved the procedures and established that the injections would be given in the back of the neck, so that the chance that the injections would harm the chicks is negligible. On this basis the great rabbis ruled that there is no need to be concerned that the injections render the birds tereifa, for the poultry growers and the companies that handle administering the injections want to make a profit, and consequently take care to perform the injections properly in a way that will not harm the chicks (Yabi'a Omer 7, YD 3).

Still, some are concerned that the injections may render the birds tereifa, and therefore there are kashrut committees that ruled to inject in the thigh (shok), and they station a mashgiaḥ to supervise this. On the other hand, there are kashrut committees that found that injections in the thigh may cause inflammations, which can dissolve sinews of the tzomet ha-gidim and render the bird tereifa (below, section 14), and therefore they ruled to inject with a short needle in the breast, in a place where there is thick flesh, and they station a mashgiaḥ to supervise this.

And although the main view is that of the great rabbis, that there is no need to be concerned about the injections, in practice, following the concerns of the stringent, it was established that the injections are given with short needles that cannot render the bird tereifa.13

notes_en.en:
The question of the injections was discussed by Rav Ovadia Yosef during his tenure as Chief Rabbi with the great rabbis: Rav Yisraeli, Rav Elyashiv, Rav Ben-Tziyon Abba Shaul, Rav Zolty and Rav Goldschmidt, as cited in Yabi'a Omer 7, YD 3. They agreed that there is no concern in this, because there is a presumption that a craftsman does not damage his craft. The craftsmen here are the poultry growers and the workers who inject the vaccines, for if they harm the chicks they will lose their livelihood. Nevertheless, there are kashrut bodies that are concerned that the injections render the birds tereifa. Therefore, there are batei din tzedek that insist that the injections be in the thigh and under the supervision of a mashgiaḥ. And there were those who challenged them (Rav Yabrov [?]), that specifically in the thigh the injection may cause inflammations in the tzomet ha-gidim, and the Rema already ruled (56:9): "And we are not expert in inspecting the tzomet ha-gidim of a bird, because it is difficult to inspect, and it easily becomes tereifa. Therefore, wherever there is a wound at the place of the tzomet ha-gidim, even if it is only swollen and blood has congealed, since it required inspection and we are not expert regarding birds — it is tereifa." Therefore, according to their view, mashgiḥim must be stationed to supervise that they inject in the breast area where the flesh is thick. And Rav Moshe Bigel, in 'Ekhol Be-simḥa' 5:2, criticized the practice of the kashrut bodies that require supervision of the injection process and cause poultry to become more expensive without sufficient reason.
As a side point, it is worth examining whether a prick of a needle as thin as today's needles into the cavity of the lungs or the esophagus renders tereifa, for perhaps, since it is so thin and leaves no mark, the impression of its prick is not in the category of a hole that renders tereifa (see the book 'Ma'or La-kashrut' vol. 3, p. 146); and the cases in which the chicks were harmed were because they were not protected from infections, and not because of the hole.

sections.title_en: Transporting Poultry and Care Not to Drop Them
sections.body_en:
When transferring the birds from the coop to the slaughterhouse, one must put the birds into a cage, load it onto a truck, and unload the cage at the slaughterhouse, and perform all these actions gently. For if the domestic animal or bird falls from a height of ten tefaḥim (about 76 cm), or is suddenly slammed down from a lower height, there is a concern that one of its organs may be injured and it will become tereifa. If the fallen creature walked on its own, walking well — this is a sign that it is kosher. And if it did not walk, but stood up, or remained twenty-four hours and did not die, one must check all its organs after the sheḥita. And if it was slaughtered before it stood up or before twenty-four hours had passed, it is tereifa, and checking will not help it, because we are concerned that it may have a defect that renders it tereifa that will not be found in the check (SA YD 58:1-6).

In practice, the work of loading the birds is difficult, because the birds may thrash about and scratch the workers. And there are workers who lose their patience and vent their anger on the birds violently, stepping on them and slamming them into the cage, and then those birds require inspection. Also when unloading the cages, it happens that a cage falls, and then all the birds in it require inspection.

The better the supervision, the more care is taken that the workers act calmly and are careful, when loading and unloading the cages, that the cage does not fall. In 5772 (2012) the Ministry of Agriculture enacted regulations on how to collect and transport the birds in a manner that reduces their suffering and eliminates the concern of their becoming tereifa. It follows that today good supervision must oversee the implementation of the regulations.

sections.title_en: The Pace of Sheḥita and Checking the Knives
sections.body_en:
The basic ruling in checking the knives was that before and after each sheḥita the shoḥet should check the knife with great concentration and attention, on its three sides, back and forth, both with the fingernail and with the flesh of the finger. And if after the sheḥita a nick is found in the knife, we are concerned that the hide of the animal or bird may have nicked the knife, and the sheḥita was invalid (above 18:6). However, with poultry it is not worthwhile to check the knife after each sheḥita, for the cost of the time spent checking is greater than the price of many birds, and it is preferable that if a nick is found in the knife, all the birds slaughtered with that knife since its previous check be declared tereifa. Therefore, they established that the knife is checked approximately every half hour. The stricter the supervision, the more care is taken to shorten the time between checks, and they take care to keep separately the birds that each shoḥet slaughtered, so that if the knife is found nicked, they will know to throw away the birds that became tereifa through him.

However, in practice, as long as the shoḥet is reliable and God-fearing, there is not much need to be particular about this, because our knives today are made of strong metal, and there is almost no chance that they will become disqualified during sheḥita. For the nick that disqualifies is one that 'catches', that is, if a hair were passed over the knife, it would get caught at the place of the nick (Ḥullin 17b; SA YD 18:2), and the chance that such a nick will be caused to the knife in the course of the sheḥitot is negligible. The reason the Sages elaborated on the laws of checking the knives is that according to the strict law, in a time of need, it is permitted to slaughter with knives of stone or wood, and it was necessary to make sure that they had no nick. Even metal knives in the past were not so sharp, as shown by the fact that the Sages instructed to check them both with the fingernail and with the flesh of the finger, and in recent generations they check them with the fingernail only, because checking them on the flesh causes cuts on the finger (above 18:6).

Another matter that is debated is the pace of sheḥita. On the one hand, the faster one slaughters, the lower the cost of the bird. On the other hand, the faster the sheḥita, the greater the concern that instead of slaughtering with a forward stroke without any pressure, the shoḥet will press the knife into the neck and render the bird tereifa through 'derasa' (SA YD 24:1-6; above 18:2). Likewise, after the sheḥita the shoḥet must see that he slaughtered properly (SA YD 25:1; above 18:2, n. 1), and the more he hurries, the harder it is for him to see that he slaughtered properly.

In ordinary slaughterhouses today, about 15-20 birds are slaughtered per minute; the meticulous slaughter up to 12 per minute, and the more meticulous slaughter up to 10 birds per minute. In addition, care is taken that the shoḥetim slaughter continuously for half an hour and rest for half an hour, and in the stringent supervisions care is taken that the shoḥetim work at most six hours a day, so that they can rest from their work and be focused when they slaughter. However, even in ordinary supervisions, as long as the shoḥet is trustworthy, even though he slaughters very quickly, there is no concern that he will press the knife or not cut the simanim, since with the sharp and strong knives we have today, the act of sheḥita is done very easily without any need to press.

Therefore, one may rely on the supervision of any authorized rabbinate, and only in very rare cases, when it becomes clear that a certain kashrut body is acting not in accordance with halakha, is it publicly announced that one should no longer rely on it.

The tzomet ha-gidim is a braid (group) of sinews extending from the muscles of the shank to the lower part of the leg. In a bird's leg this braid includes sixteen sinews, by means of which the bird directs the movement of its leg and toes. If one of these sinews is torn — the bird is tereifa (SA YD 56:8). However, from the days of the Sages until our day no need arose to inspect them; rather, they were treated like all the seventy-two tereifot in birds, regarding which we follow the overwhelming majority, which is kosher. Only if a 'ri'uta' (abnormality) arose, that is, a certain problem in the appearance of a particular place, was it necessary to inspect it. However, in the last generation more cases of torn sinews in the tzomet ha-gidim have begun to be discovered. The reason for this is a contagious disease that causes inflammations in the sinews, and when the birds are raised in crowded conditions, the disease may spread and infect many birds. In practice, even today, when this problem has become more common, only one percent of all birds have a torn sinew, and most flocks are entirely free of this problem, and on rare occasions there are flocks in which the percentage of problems reaches tens of percent.

Some say that since the overall percentage of problems is a 'mi'ut she-eino matzui', and this defect is difficult to identify, there is no need to inspect the tzomet ha-gidim at all (Minḥat Yitzḥak 8:65). On the other hand, some say that since there are sometimes flocks in which a 'mi'ut ha-matzui' has damage to the tzomet ha-gidim, all the birds must be inspected (Shevet Ha-levi 4:81). In practice, it appears that since there are sometimes flocks with problems, and it is not difficult to perform a sample inspection, it is proper to inspect each flock by sampling, and if birds with torn sinews are found in it, all the birds in the flock should be inspected, and if none are found — there will be no need to inspect the birds in it. And the stringent inspect all the birds in any case.

Another question arose: how to inspect the tzomet ha-gidim. Some take the trouble to cut the legs of all the birds and stretch the sinews to see that they are intact. On the other hand, rabbis and experts argue that this inspection is not effective, because if there is a torn sinew, the cutting interferes with seeing it. And some even hold that since only a few are expert in inspecting the tzomet ha-gidim from the inside, it is better not to open the leg in order to inspect it, but rather to look at the place from the outside, and if by sight and touch it appears to have thickened, it is likely that it became inflamed and has torn sinews. In practice, both methods disqualify the same percentage of birds, but according to those who inspect from the outside, the decisions of those who cut the shank are less accurate.14

notes_en.en: The issue is explained in the books 'Ma'or La-kashrut' part 3, p. 156, and 'Ekhol Be-simḥa' 5:3, pp. 81-82. In Minḥat Yitzḥak 8:65 he wrote that since the frequency of problems in the tzomet ha-gidim is very low (about one percent or less), there is no need to inspect the birds without a specific abnormality. And according to Shevet Ha-levi (4:81), all the birds must be inspected; but since only a few know how to inspect the sinews properly with an internal inspection, and there is a concern that the inspector will identify a problem and mistakenly declare it kosher, it is better not to perform an internal inspection at all but only an external inspection, just as the Rema wrote (33:9): "And it would be better not to inspect at all and rely on the majority, than to inspect and be lenient where there is an abnormality." And this is also the opinion of Rav Werner. And it appears that in practice an external inspection is preferable.

sections.body_en:
A similar question arose regarding the inspection of the lungs of poultry. In principle, the basic ruling was that one does not inspect for the seventy tereifot of domestic animals and the seventy-two of birds, except for the lungs of domestic animals (SA YD 39:1). However, on rare occasions an epidemic breaks out that affects the lungs of the birds, making them hard as wood, or swollen, or changing their appearance to the color of flesh, or they have bubbles or growths on them that render them tereifa (SA YD 36-38). However, the percentage of tereifot from this out of all the birds is very low, less than one percent, so that according to the strict law there is no obligation to inspect the lungs of birds. However, since in certain flocks the percentage of tereifot is higher, and it is not difficult to perform a sample inspection for each flock, it is proper to perform it.

Today there is a machine that removes the internal organs of the bird and hangs them on a conveyor belt, and the mashgiaḥ can easily look at the lungs as at the other internal organs. If in the sample inspection he sees that the flock has no lung problem, there is no need to continue inspecting the lungs in that flock. And if it is found that a certain percentage has problems, the lungs of all the birds should be inspected. The stringent customarily inspect the lungs of all the birds, with some inspecting them quickly and some deliberately.15

Some are meticulous to inspect the legs of the birds to see whether they were dislocated from their place (buka de-atma, the hip socket), for if they were dislocated — the bird is tereifa (SA YD 55:2). However, according to halakha, since this problem is rare, there is no need to check for it, and only if in the course of handling the birds a bird was seen to have been injured in this way should it be declared tereifa.

notes_en.en: There is no obligation to inspect the lungs of a bird, as the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Sheḥita 11:12): "And we have never heard of anyone who inspected a bird, unless a concern arose." However, when birds are raised in large flocks, sometimes a disease spreads that affects the lungs of many birds. However, since overall the percentage of birds whose lungs are affected is very low, there is no obligation to inspect them (as explained above, section 4). And even if we know of a flock that has problems at the level of a 'mi'ut ha-matzui', since there is a doubt whether these are problems that render tereifa, the poskim disagreed whether there is an obligation to inspect. According to Mishkenot Ya'akov (YD 17) one must inspect, and according to Beit Efrayim (YD 6) one need not. It follows that by Torah law there is in any case no obligation to inspect, since most birds are kosher. And by rabbinic law too it is a sefek sefeika: it is doubtful whether this flock has problems at the level of a mi'ut ha-matzui, and even if there are problems, it is doubtful whether one must inspect because of them; therefore there is no obligation to inspect birds (and so wrote Even Yisrael 2, Sheḥita 7). And some instruct to inspect all the birds (Shevet Ha-levi 2:14-15).

sections.title_en: Questions About Poultry Sold with a Hekhsher
sections.body_en:
Sometimes one who buys a bird with a hekhsher finds in one of its bones a fracture that may be one of the fractures that render the bird tereifa. However, since many of the fractures are caused after the sheḥita by plucking the feathers or by the bird falling, these fractures pose no problem. But on very rare occasions, one finds that the area around the fracture looks very black or very red because of a great deal of blood that congealed there, and then there is a concern that the fracture occurred while the bird was alive and perhaps it renders the bird tereifa. Therefore, without asking a sage who is familiar with these laws, such a bird should not be declared kosher.

One who buys a bird that was salted and kashered and finds in it congealed blood, that is, a place in the meat in which actual blood has congealed, must cut it out and throw it away (below 22:4). And if there is a doubt whether there is actual congealed blood there or only a red color that remained after the salting, there is no need to cut it out.

If there was definitely congealed blood there, and he erred and did not cut it out and cooked the bird — the bird is kosher. This is because it is not certain whether the congealed blood formed before the kashering of the meat, in which case it is forbidden, or after it, in which case it is not forbidden. And since cooked blood is forbidden by rabbinic law (below 22:2, n. 4), in a situation of doubt one should be lenient.
